exercise.title: Why do complex numbers live in a plane?

statement.p: A complex number z=a+bi is drawn as the point (a,b). In your own words, why does solving x^2+1=0 force a second direction off the real line, and what do the real and imaginary parts record geometrically?

hint.p: No real number squares to -1, so a new axis is opened. Horizontal position is the real part; vertical position is the imaginary part. Addition then looks like vector addition.

statement.p: Complex arithmetic is ordinary algebra, together with the rule i^2=-1.

exercise.title: What extra information does polar form record?

statement.p: Polar form writes z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta). In your own words, why are length and angle a natural pair of coordinates, and why is the argument of a nonzero complex number not unique?

hint.p: A point not at the origin is determined by how far it is from the origin and which way it points. Turning all the way around the circle returns to the same point, so \theta and \theta+2\pi describe the same direction.

exercise.title: Why does complex multiplication rotate and scale?

statement.p: In polar form, moduli multiply and arguments add. In your own words, why is that the geometric meaning of zw, and why does multiplication by i turn every complex number by a quarter-turn?

hint.p: The angle-addition formulas are exactly the real and imaginary parts of the product. The number i has length 1 and angle \pi/2, so it preserves length and adds a right angle.

statement.p: The number i has polar form
Multiplying by i preserves length and adds angle \pi/2. Therefore multiplication by i rotates every complex number counterclockwise by 90^\circ.
The point (a,b) becomes (-b,a), which is a 90^\circ counterclockwise rotation.

figure.caption: Multiplication by i rotates a complex number counterclockwise by 90^\circ.

statement.p: Polar form turns multiplication into geometry. This is the reason complex numbers are so useful for oscillation: oscillation is repeated rotation.

exercise.title: Why does Euler’s formula fall out of Taylor series?

statement.p: Defining e^z by the same power series as the real exponential, and substituting z=i\theta, splits the series into the cosine series plus i times the sine series. In your own words, why do the powers of i create that split, and why is the resulting identity more than a coincidence of formulas?

hint.p: The cycle 1,i,-1,-i sends even powers to the real axis and odd powers to the imaginary axis, with the familiar alternating signs. The exponential series is then visibly the rotating point \cos\theta+i\sin\theta.

exercise.title: Why is e^{it} the natural language of oscillation?

statement.p: As t changes, e^{it} moves around the unit circle, with velocity a quarter-turn of position and acceleration pointing back to the origin. In your own words, why does that make sine and cosine shadows of one rotation, rather than two unrelated waves?

hint.p: The real part is cosine and the imaginary part is sine. Differentiating multiplies by i, which rotates the velocity onto the tangent. Differentiating again multiplies by -1, which is the geometry of circular motion.
